Mississippi Stud Basics: The 3-2-1 Raise Pattern

Published October 3, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Mississippi Stud looks intimidating the first time you watch a table play it — five cards get revealed one at a time, and the dealer keeps asking players to decide whether to add money before most of the hand is even visible. Underneath that unfamiliar rhythm, though, it's a fairly simple game built around one repeating idea: you get more chances to bet, but each chance costs you a shrinking amount of information. Once that structure clicks, the game stops feeling like a guessing exercise and starts feeling like a series of small, learnable decisions.

  2. The 3-2-1 raise pattern explained

How a hand actually unfolds

Every hand starts the same way: you place an ante bet, and the dealer gives you two cards face up. No community cards are visible yet, so your entire decision at this point rests on just those two cards. From there, the dealer reveals three community cards one at a time, and after each reveal, you get a chance to either add a bet ("raise") or give up your hand ("fold"). Your final hand, like most poker-based table games, is the best five-card combination you can make from your two cards plus the three community cards everyone at the table shares.

That shared-community-card detail matters for how you read the table: everyone is building their final hand from the same three revealed cards, so a strong community card (say, a pair showing on the felt) improves every active player's hand simultaneously, not just yours.

The 3-2-1 raise pattern explained

This is the detail that gives the game its personality. At each of the three decision points, the maximum raise you're allowed to make gets smaller as more of the hand gets revealed:

Decision pointWhat's visibleMaximum raise allowed
1st decisionYour 2 cards only, no community cardsUp to 3× your ante
2nd decisionYour 2 cards + 1st community cardUp to 2× your ante
3rd decisionYour 2 cards + 2nd community cardUp to 1× your ante
Final cardAll 5 cards visible, no more raises — hand is settledNot applicable

The logic is straightforward once you see it laid out: the less certainty you have about your final hand, the more the casino lets you risk if you're confident enough to take the bigger swing. By the time you reach the third decision, you've seen four of your five cards, so there's far less unknown left — which is exactly why the house caps your remaining raise at a single unit instead of three.

Takeaway: The 3-2-1 raise cap isn't a trick — it's the game's whole structure in miniature. Betting bigger early, when you know the least, is the entire design concept.

The pay table: what beats a pair of 6s

Your ante and every raise you've made get paid out together based on your final five-card hand, using a pay table that starts at a pair of 6s or better. Anything weaker than a pair of 6s (a pair of 2s through 5s, or no pair at all) loses both the ante and any raises you placed. A typical pay table looks like this:

Final handTypical payout
Royal flush500 to 1
Straight flush100 to 1
Four of a kind40 to 1
Full house10 to 1
Flush6 to 1
Straight4 to 1
Three of a kind3 to 1
Two pair2 to 1
Pair of 6s or better1 to 1 (even money)
Pair of 2s–5s or worseLoses ante and all raises

Exact payout tables can vary slightly by casino or online operator, so it's worth glancing at the table posted at the game you're playing before you sit down — the structure above is the standard most tables use, but a slightly weaker pay table (lower flush or straight payouts, for instance) will push the house edge a bit higher than the figures discussed later in this guide.

Why folding too early is the real leak, not folding itself

Here's the part that surprises a lot of new players: Mississippi Stud is actually a fairly fold-friendly game by casino-table standards, because you only ever lose your ante (plus whatever you've already raised) — you're never forced to match a bigger bet just to see the next card. That structure might make folding feel "safe" by default, and it leads a lot of players to fold more often than the math actually supports, especially on the first decision when only two cards are visible.

The real leak isn't folding in general — it's folding hands that basic strategy says to play. Because every raise you make is paid out at even money or better if you win, and because the community cards give you three more looks at improving your hand, several two-card starting hands that feel unpromising (a single high card, for instance) are still worth a 1x raise at minimum under correct strategy, simply because the payout math on the back end more than compensates for the modest risk up front.

Basic strategy touchpoints at each street

Full Mississippi Stud strategy runs through dozens of specific card combinations, but the broad shape looks like this:

First decision (your 2 cards only): Raise 3x with a pair of any rank, or with two cards that are both 3 or higher (giving you reasonable straight and flush potential). Fold hands with no pair and at least one card below a 3 and no realistic path to a pair of 6s or better.

Second decision (1 community card showing): Raise if the new card gives you or keeps alive a pair of 6s or better, a made straight or flush draw with live outs, or three cards to a straight flush. Fold hands that still show no realistic path to the pay table's minimum qualifying hand.

Third decision (2 community cards showing): This is the easiest decision of the three, because you've seen four of your five cards. Raise if you already have a pair of 6s or better, or a strong enough draw (open-ended straight, four to a flush) that the odds of completing it justify the 1x bet. Fold everything else — at this point you have the clearest read of the hand you'll get before the final card.

Memorizing the exact chart takes repetition, but even a simplified version of this logic — bet big early with real potential, get more selective as the picture sharpens, and remember that even a modest made hand at the final decision point is usually worth the last 1x raise — captures most of the value of full strategy.

The actual house edge, and how it's measured

Game analysts commonly cite the house edge on Mississippi Stud at a little under 5% of total action — that is, measured against everything you put at risk across the ante and all three potential raises, assuming you play every decision with correct strategy. That number sits in the same general neighborhood as many other poker-based table games like Three Card Poker or Ultimate Texas Hold'em, though direct comparisons are imperfect since each game structures its raises differently.

Two things push that number around in practice. Playing loose with starting hands (raising hands strategy says to fold) or playing too tight (folding hands strategy says to raise) both increase the effective edge you're giving up, often substantially more than the baseline figure. And because the game lets you raise up to 3x your ante multiple times, your total action — and therefore your total expected loss in dollar terms — can run well above your ante alone, which is worth factoring into bankroll planning the same way you would for any multiplier-heavy table game. Frequently asked questions

What's the minimum hand that actually pays in Mississippi Stud?

A pair of 6s or better pays even money on your ante and any raises. A pair of 2s, 3s, 4s, or 5s — or no pair at all — loses everything you've put in, even though you technically made a pair.

Why does the maximum raise shrink from 3x to 2x to 1x?

It mirrors how much you know about your final hand. At the first decision you've seen only 2 of your 5 cards, so the casino allows a bigger swing; by the third decision you've seen 4 of 5 cards, so the remaining uncertainty — and the allowed raise — is much smaller.

Is it better to fold often in Mississippi Stud since you can lose less?

No — folding more than correct strategy calls for is one of the most common mistakes in the game. Because winning hands pay even money or better and you get three looks at improving your cards, several starting hands that feel weak are still worth a raise under the math.

How does Mississippi Stud's house edge compare to blackjack or baccarat?

It's higher. Blackjack with correct basic strategy and baccarat's banker bet both run under 1.5%, while Mississippi Stud's commonly cited edge sits closer to 5% of total action with perfect strategy — more in line with other poker-based table games than with the lowest-edge games in the casino.
